title: Stored-program computing to reusable software and compatible System/360 platform
pressure: Electronic speed was of limited value when each machine required bespoke configuration, scarce memory and machine-specific programming. Institutions needed computers that could store programs, support reusable software and later preserve investment across a family of compatible machines.
preExistingWorldModel: Wartime electronic machines had shown high-speed calculation/search, but many were special-purpose or manually reconfigured. Stored-program ideas existed on paper before practical working machines; early computers also differed radically in word length, instruction sets, peripherals and programming conventions.
candidateRoutes: program-controlled machines with externally configured instructions
practical stored-program service machines with reusable subroutine libraries
high-level compiled languages over machine-specific hardware
compatible families sharing architecture and software across performance tiers
observationsAndInstruments: The Manchester Baby executed a stored program in 1948 as an experimental proof of stored-program operation.
EDSAC in 1949 moved stored-program computing into a practical service environment and developed subroutine-library practices.
FORTRAN demonstrated that a compiler could translate higher-level scientific programs into efficient machine code, reducing direct dependence on instruction-level programming.
IBM System/360 in 1964 deliberately offered a family of mutually compatible computers across a wide performance range, making software/peripheral compatibility an explicit product-system property.
Time-sharing and interactive systems in the 1960s exposed new requirements for responsiveness, protection, scheduling and shared software beyond batch computation.
decisiveTests: A stored-program machine had to execute instructions from rewritable memory reliably rather than merely embody the idea in a design document.
Reusable libraries/compilers had to reduce programming burden while producing useful running programs.
System/360 compatibility had to work across materially different models so customer software and peripheral investment could survive hardware upgrades.
technicalOrScientificTransition: Computing moved from proving electronic/stored-program execution toward reusable software and then toward architecture compatibility as a platform property. The unit of value widened from a fast machine to a machine-plus-software-plus-peripheral ecosystem.
rivalsAndFailures: Stored-program execution did not instantly eliminate special-purpose computers, which remained efficient for stable workloads.
High-level languages reduced machine dependence but created compiler/runtime complexity and did not make hardware differences disappear.
Compatibility can preserve customer investment but also constrains later design freedom; it is not free generality.
diffusionAndScaling: Stored-program computing became normal during the 1950s; reusable software and high-level languages broadened access; System/360-scale architectural compatibility turned computer families into long-lived institutional platforms in the 1960s.
standardsAndInstitutions: Manchester University, Cambridge, IBM, user organizations, universities, government procurement and software communities progressively divided hardware, software, operations and compatibility responsibilities.
externalitiesAndCorrections: Large centralized computer systems also concentrated organizational dependency and access; broader privacy/security consequences become more explicit in later networked epochs.
secondOrderEffects: Reusable programming abstractions and compatible architectures lowered the cost of building future applications and made software itself a durable engineering asset.
sourceNativeSummary: HD5 computing is a transition in what must remain stable: first instructions move into memory, then routines/languages become reusable, then architecture compatibility preserves software and peripheral investment across machines. A “faster computer” metric misses this platform transition.
unresolvedHistoricalQuestions: How much System/360 success should be attributed to technical compatibility versus IBM sales/service/institutional power?
Which early software abstractions genuinely transferred across machines versus remaining vendor-local?
